introduction-the-digital-supply-chain.core: Data pipelines are the supply chain of data: they extract raw data from many sources, transform it into useful shapes, and load it where analytics and AI can use it, either in scheduled batches or as continuous streams.

first_principles.problem: Data sits scattered across logs, databases and SaaS tools, so no one can answer cross-system questions or train models on it.
truths: Data is produced in many places.
Consumers need it clean and combined.
derivation: Use **streaming** (Flink, Kafka Streams) for real-time needs.
Handle **windows, state and time**; pick tools with a **framework**.

analogy.title: A factory supply chain
analogy.story: Raw materials are collected from suppliers, processed in factories and delivered to stores.
analogy.breaks: Unlike physical goods, data can be copied endlessly, so governance and lineage matter.

check.q: What are the three steps of a data pipeline?
check.a: Extract from sources, transform into useful shapes, and load into destinations.

two-paradigms-etl-vs-elt.core: ETL transforms data before loading it (on separate compute). ELT loads raw data into a powerful warehouse first and transforms it there with SQL (dbt). Cheap cloud warehouses made ELT the modern default, because raw data is kept and transformations are easy to change.

first_principles.problem: ETL pipelines discard raw data, so new questions require re-extracting from sources.
truths: Warehouse compute is now cheap and elastic.
derivation: **ETL**: transform in flight, load curated data (good for strict PII filtering).
**ELT**: load raw, transform in the warehouse (dbt models).

analogy.title: Cooking before shopping vs. stocking the pantry
analogy.story: ETL cooks the meal at the market and brings home only the dish; ELT brings home ingredients and cooks whatever you need later.
analogy.breaks: ELT can land sensitive raw data in the warehouse, so mask PII early.

batch-processing-the-heavy-lifter.core: Batch processing handles large, bounded datasets in scheduled chunks (nightly aggregates, training-set builds), using distributed engines like Spark that split data into partitions across many machines.

first_principles.problem: Processing terabytes on one machine takes days or runs out of memory.
truths: Partitions can be processed in parallel.
Many questions don't need real-time answers.
derivation: Make jobs **idempotent** so they can be re-run safely.

analogy.title: Counting toll-booth cars for a year
analogy.story: Count each day's tally in parallel, then sum them, rather than counting one car at a time live.
analogy.breaks: Batch latency (hours) is unacceptable for fraud or real-time personalisation.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Terabytes processed in minutes across a cluster.

check.q: Why should batch jobs be idempotent?
check.a: So they can be safely re-run after failures without duplicating or corrupting results.

spark-internals-rdds-vs-dataframes-and-t.core: Spark evolved from RDDs (low-level, opaque functions Spark can't optimise) to DataFrames and Datasets (structured, declarative). With DataFrames the Catalyst optimizer rewrites your query plan (predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering) and Tungsten generates efficient code.

first_principles.problem: Hand-written RDD code is slow because Spark can't see inside your lambdas to optimise them.
derivation: **Tungsten** executes it with code generation; inspect with `explain()`.

analogy.title: Giving a taxi driver the destination vs. turn-by-turn orders
analogy.story: With the destination (declarative), the driver picks the fastest route; with fixed turns (RDD), they can't optimise.
analogy.breaks: Python UDFs are opaque to Catalyst too, so prefer built-in functions.

check.q: Why are DataFrames usually faster than RDDs in Spark?
check.a: Their declarative structure lets the Catalyst optimizer rewrite and optimise the query plan, which opaque RDD functions prevent.

stream-processing-the-need-for-now.core: Stream processing handles unbounded data continuously, event by event or in small windows, for fraud detection, real-time recommendations, monitoring and alerting, with latencies in milliseconds to seconds.

first_principles.problem: A fraud model that runs on last night's batch catches fraud a day too late.
truths: Some decisions lose value over time.
Infinite data needs different computation models.
derivation: Process with a **stream engine** (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming).
Use **windows** for aggregates, and keep **state** for context.

analogy.title: A live news ticker vs. the morning paper
analogy.story: The ticker updates as events happen; the paper summarises yesterday.
analogy.breaks: Streaming adds complexity (state, ordering, exactly-once), so use it only when freshness matters.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fraud is stopped before it completes.

example.outcome: decisions made while they still matter.

points: Use it only when freshness matters.

check.q: When is stream processing worth its complexity?
check.a: When decisions lose value quickly, as in fraud detection, real-time recommendations or alerting.

flink-concept-1-windowing-and-state.core: You can't average an infinite stream, so windows chop it into finite chunks: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) and session (gap-based). Keyed state (per user or card) lets operators remember context, checkpointed for fault tolerance.

first_principles.problem: 'Average spend per user' has no meaning on an endless stream without boundaries and memory.

analogy.title: Counting cars in time slots
analogy.story: Count per 10-minute slot (tumbling), keep a rolling last-hour count (sliding), or count per convoy (session).
analogy.breaks: Large state increases checkpoint time and recovery cost.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bounded aggregates over an unbounded stream.

check.q: What's the difference between tumbling and sliding windows?
check.a: Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping; sliding windows overlap and advance in smaller steps.

flink-concept-2-the-problem-of-time-and-.core: Event time (when something happened) differs from processing time (when the system sees it), because of network delays and mobile offline queues. Watermarks declare 'no events older than T are expected', letting windows close correctly while still tolerating some lateness.

first_principles.problem: Windows computed on processing time put late-arriving events in the wrong bucket, so results are wrong.
truths: Waiting forever for stragglers isn't possible.
derivation: Close windows when the **watermark passes** the end.

analogy.title: Collecting exam papers by a deadline
analogy.story: Papers sent by post arrive late; you set a cut-off and decide what to do with stragglers.
analogy.breaks: Watermarks trade latency for completeness, so tune them to your data's lateness.

example.outcome: correct results despite messy arrival times.

check.q: What does a watermark tell a stream processor?
check.a: That it shouldn't expect events with timestamps older than a given time, so windows up to that point can be finalised.

a-note-on-kafka-streams.core: Kafka Streams is a library, not a cluster: stream processing runs inside your own Java/Kotlin application, reading and writing Kafka topics, with state in local RocksDB stores backed by changelog topics. It scales by adding app instances.

first_principles.problem: Running a Spark or Flink cluster is overkill for a moderate streaming transformation in one service.
truths: Kafka already provides durability and partitioning.
derivation: **State stores** are local RocksDB + changelog topics.

analogy.title: A food truck vs. a restaurant kitchen
analogy.story: For a simple menu, a self-contained truck beats building a whole commercial kitchen.
analogy.breaks: It's JVM-only and Kafka-only, and complex multi-source jobs fit Flink better.

check.q: What's the main operational advantage of Kafka Streams over Flink?
check.a: It runs as a library inside your application, with no separate processing cluster to operate.

choosing-the-right-tool-a-decision-frame.core: Choose by latency need (hours → batch Spark/dbt, seconds → streaming), data volume and complexity (Flink for complex stateful multi-source, Kafka Streams for simple Kafka-native, Spark for large batch and ML) and team skills and operational capacity.

first_principles.problem: Teams pick Flink for a nightly report or Spark batch for real-time fraud.
derivation: Ask **how big and complex** it is.
Default to the **simplest tool** that meets the need.

analogy.title: Choosing transport
analogy.story: A cargo ship for bulk (batch), a courier bike for urgent small parcels (streaming).
analogy.breaks: Unified engines (Spark Structured Streaming, Flink batch) blur the lines.
